identity.name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
native_names: กรุงเทพทวารวดีศรีอยุธยา (Krung Thep Dvaravati Si Ayutthaya)

land.text: Lopburi and Ayodhya, the Lavo core

No Cliopatria row; the Suphanburi line took the throne in 1370 (Borommarachathirat) and again in 1408 (Intharacha).

land.text: Phip Phli (Phetchaburi), named in the infobox among the predecessors

The infobox also names Phimai, Phitsanulok, Sawangburi and Nakhon Si Thammarat among the preceding and succeeding states without saying which are which (see notes).

The page gives no extent for 1351-1374; the rendering agent should draw the four cities' provinces. The 1375 jump to 288,685 km2 is not dated by the page (see ledger).

keyframe_review.note: 288,685 km2, 0.72 of the infobox 400,000 km2. Of its 909 new cells 680 lie in Cliopatria's Sukhothai outline of 1374, 212 in the Khmer Empire's, 13 in Lavo's. The Sukhothai page has Sukhothai a tributary of Ayutthaya from 1378 ('Tributary of Ayutthaya: 1378-1438') and annexed only in 1438, with Song Khwae (Phitsanulok) its capital 1347-1438, so Phitsanulok, Kamphaeng Phet and the other Northern Cities are not direct Ayutthayan land in 1375-1437: drawn as a vassal tint (vassal_start 1378). Tenasserim and the peninsula stay as Cliopatria draws them, a tributary claim: the Ayutthaya page has expeditions 'to demand tribute from Malay principalities' in 1290s-1490s but no 1375 conquest. The 13 Lavo cells are the ledger's 1375 gain from lavo-kingdom.

The Ayutthaya page says Lavo was 'fully incorporated' in 1388, so those cells belong to Ayutthaya from 1388, not 1395 (new keyframe 1388). Years 1395-1437: the same Northern Cities correction as 1375; Sukhothai is annexed in 1438 (new keyframe 1438).

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1438-1449: Sukhothai 'was annexed by the kingdom in 1438 after the death of Borommapan'; Cliopatria draws Sukhothai's core as Ayutthaya's only from 1450 (212 of its 215 cells). The page also says Baker and Pasuk reject the older account of conquest or absorption and that 'Personal Union with Ayutthaya: 1438-1569': drawn as direct land, as the Sukhothai page's own 1438 end implies.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1450 shape, which holds Sukhothai's core and the Northern Cities, from the 1438 annexation

keyframe_review.note: 383,905 km2, 0.96 of the infobox 400,000 km2. The 213 new cells (Tak, Nan, Lampang, Phrae, Uttaradit, Sukhothai, part of Chiang Mai) are Cliopatria's Sukhothai core. The Lan Na war page has Tilokaraj capture 'the cities of Phrae and Muong Nan' (no year) and Ayutthaya reconquer Phrae only in 1460, so Phrae and Nan are at best contested in 1441-1474: the ledger's contest_start 1441 / contest_end 1474 carries that.

383,598 km2: one cell fewer than 1450. The war page's Sawankhalok moves (1451 to Lan Na, back to Ayutthaya, 1459 to Lan Na) are not in any Cliopatria shape; the ledger has them: 1451 loss, return placed in 1453, 1459 loss, and Ayutthaya's retaking in 1474 (Tilokaraj page).

393,651 km2 (0.98 of the infobox). The 32 new cells (Songkhla, Satun, Pattani) lie 18 in Kedah's and 13 outside any Cliopatria outline; the page dates none of it (expeditions down the peninsula 1290s-1490s). Unverified: page budget.
Two cells' difference from 1459; nothing to explain.

404,261 km2. The 36 new cells (Narathiwat, Yala, Pattani, 2 cells of Perak) are the Patani region; the Patani page says the sultanate attacked Ayutthaya in 1563, so Ayutthaya's hold was a tributary claim, drawn direct by Cliopatria. The Ayutthaya page has Malacca fall to the Portuguese in 1511, which is the context, not a cause on the page. Adjusted in the repair pass: the Patani strip (36 cells) is drawn as a vassal tint 1512-1528; the Patani page has the region 'subject to Siamese control for some time' before 1563 but no conquest or date, and Patani attacked Ayutthaya in 1563.

keyframe_review.note: 393,604 km2: 36 western cells (Tanintharyi 16, Kayin 7, Mon 7, Kanchanaburi 4, Tak 2) go in 1564, the year of the surrender on 18 February 1564. But the 1568-1569 war page says 'The Burmese first took Phitsanulok, Sawankhalok, Kamphaeng Phet, Sukhothai thus turning them into tributary states' in the 1563 war, and Phitsanulok was 'a Burmese vassal state' in 1568: the Northern Cities leave in 1563-1564 and are not Ayutthaya's until 1584. Years 1564-1571; Ayutthaya itself is Toungoo's vassal from 18 February 1564 (infobox 'Suzerain of Siam: 18 February 1564 - 10 October 1581'), which first-toungoo-empire's dossier should carry as vassal_start. The Patani strip also leaves here: Patani attacked Ayutthaya in 1563 (Patani page), the ledger closes its vassal span in 1563, and the 1572 keyframe already lacks it.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1572-1587: Cliopatria has no Ayutthaya shape for these years, but the kingdom existed: the infobox gives 'vassal of the Toungoo dynasty' 1564-68 and 1569-84 and 'May 1584: Naresuan proclaims independence'. Same extent as 1588 without the Northern Cities until they return in 1584 (the Sukhothai page: 'Annexed to Ayutthaya: 1584'); the Patani cells are absent because the Patani vassal span ended in 1563 (ledger), which agrees with Cliopatria's Patani row beginning in 1572.

keyframe_review.note: 382,305 km2 (0.96 of the infobox): the Patani cells (Yala, Narathiwat, Pattani, 2 of Perak) are absent because the Patani vassal span ended in 1563 (ledger) and Cliopatria's Patani row begins in 1572. The Patani page has Raja Hijau 'acknowledged Siamese authority' in 1584: a vassal, see the ledger.

432,494 km2 (1.08 of the infobox). The 165 new cells follow the war page: Tenasserim, Tavoy and Mergui in 1593, 'The Mon provinces then became subject to Siam' in 1594 (Kayin 71, Mon 32, Tanintharyi 16). But 31 of the cells lie in Bago and Yangon: Naresuan besieged Pegu from January 1595 for about three months and 'withdrew', and the page does not give him the city.

keyframe_review.note: 450,375 km2 (1.13 of the infobox), the largest. The 58 new cells are Bago (36) and Kayin (22): 'Pegu was abandoned and burned before Naresuan arrived', he marched on Toungoo and 'in May 1600, he gave up the fight'. The infobox says he regained 'Lan Na and Tanintharyi region'; Lan Na is a vassal here, not in the shape. Years 1600-1618.

keyframe_review.note: 382,305 km2. 1613 Burma takes Tavoy; 1614 invades Lan Na; the 1618 treaty gives Burma Lan Na and leaves Ayutthaya southern Tanintharyi. The shape drops the Mon provinces and Bago (222 cells) but keeps 99 of 119 Tanintharyi cells, more than 'southern Tanintharyi'; the page gives no more.

420,187 km2: 126 cells (Kayin 67, Mon 29, Tanintharyi 16, Tak, Kanchanaburi) for 1662-1669. The war page: Narai took Chiang Mai in February 1663, invaded Burma in November 1663 with Tavoy, Martaban and Moulmein as objectives (taking Tavoy is not confirmed), withdrew by May 1664, and the Tenasserim cities 'fell back almost immediately under Burmese rule'. Nothing held to 1669. Years 1662-1669 use the 1619 outline (the 1670 shape); the 1663-1664 fighting is a contest.

correction.text: Ayutthaya as in 1619-1661 and 1670-1690; the Mon strip was fought over in 1663-1664 and lost again

keyframe_review.note: 382,305 km2, the 1619 outline again once the Mon strip is gone: 'Burma and Siam then had peace for 95 years, until 1759'.

393,604 km2: the 39 new cells are the Patani region (Yala, Narathiwat, Pattani, 2 of Perak), handed to Ayutthaya because Cliopatria's Patani row ends in 1690. The Patani page has Patani refuse Phetracha's authority and rebel in 1688, and the sultanate goes on to Siam's conquest in 1786 ('Conquest by Siam: 1786'); nothing makes it Ayutthayan in 1691. Patani stays separate (patani-kingdom, group se-02).

415,858 km2: 70 cells (Kayin 30, Tanintharyi 16, Mon 14, Tak 5, Kanchanaburi 4) for 1752-1761. ledger.note: 1351: the Ayutthaya Kingdom is founded. The page gives 4 March 1351 as the official establishment ('the article says this date is conventional') and has Lopburi, Suphanburi, Ayodhya and Phetchaburi 'merging into one polity'; Uthong is the first king. The page names the cities, not a boundary.

region.text: Lopburi, Suphanburi, Ayodhya and Phetchaburi merged into one polity before 1351

ledger.note: 1353: Ayutthaya takes Angkor and sets its princes on the Khmer throne. 'Angkor was besieged by the Ayutthayan king Uthong in 1352', and 'following its capture the next year, the Khmer king was replaced with successive Siamese princes'; the Ramathibodi I page agrees ('He was successful the following year and placed one of his sons on the throne'). The Ayutthaya page says the army took 'captives and goods rather than annexing the city': the occupation is the Khmer page's reading, mirrored on khmer-empire /ledger/29.

region.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

ledger.note: 1357: the Khmers retake Angkor. 'Then in 1357, the Khmer king Suryavamsa Rajadhiraja retook the throne'; the Ramathibodi I page: 'they were only able to keep the throne until 1357, when the Khmers were able to regain it'. Mirrors khmer-empire /ledger/30.

region.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

ledger.note: 1370: Borommarachathirat of Suphanburi takes Ayutthaya from Ramesuan of Lopburi, who withdraws to Lavo. The page: 'Ramesuan loses Ayutthaya to Borommarachathirat' in 1370; 'Lopburi and Suphanburi rivalry 1370-1409' (infobox). Same state, a different line.

1375: Cliopatria draws a large western strip of the Khmer Empire as Ayutthaya's (212 of the 909 new cells lie in the Khmer outline of 1374). The page dates no cession; it says only that within a few years of 1351 Ramathibodi I's forces 'captured Nakhon Thom (Yasodharapura) but did not annex it'. Page silent on 1375. Ramathibodi I page: authority 'extended to Korat, Chanthaburi' (chronicles, undated); Borommarachathirat I page: no event in 1375. The 1352-53 and 1393-94 Angkor events are in the ledger as the occupation and contest.

region.text: the western strip of Cliopatria's Khmer Empire outline of 1374 that is Ayutthaya's from 1375

ledger.note: 1375: Cliopatria extends Ayutthaya over the Khorat plateau, the Malay peninsula down to Nakhon Si Thammarat and the Tenasserim coast: 680 cells of Cliopatria's Sukhothai outline of 1374 (which shrinks to a 215-cell northern core in 1375). The Ayutthaya page has expeditions 'to demand tribute from Malay principalities' in the 1290s-1490s and Tavoy, Mergui, Tenasserim and Martaban 'contested' only in the late 15th century. Page silent on 1375; a tributary claim at most. Ramathibodi I page (re-read 2026-10-19): 'According to royal chronicles, his authority extended to Korat, Chanthaburi, Tavoy, Tanintharyi' and then 'parts of Malaya', undated and before his death in 1369; the Borommarachathirat I page records no war or gain in 1375 and does not mention Khorat, the peninsula or Tenasserim. The year is Cliopatria's, so confidence stays 1. The 13 Lavo cells are carved out of this region and carried by the Lavo gain.

region.text: the central plains' outer ring: Khorat, the Malay peninsula to Nakhon Si Thammarat, Tenasserim, as Cliopatria draws 1375

ledger.note: 1375: the last 13 cells of Cliopatria's Lavo outline pass to Ayutthaya's shape. Mirrors lavo-kingdom /ledger/12 (same region, confidence 1). Page silent on 1375: the Ayutthaya page has Lavo 'not fully incorporated into Ayutthaya's political order until 1388'; the cells are bridged from the Cliopatria change.

region.text: the strip Lavo loses between 1374 and 1375 (13 cells, all inside Cliopatria's Ayutthaya shape of 1375)

ledger.note: 1378: Lue Thai of Sukhothai submits as an Ayutthayan vassal. 'in 1378 Lue Thai submitted as a vassal'; infobox 'Tributary of Ayutthaya: 1378-1438'; 'In 1349 armies from Ayutthaya invaded and made Sukhothai a tributary' is the page's earlier, lapsed tribute. The page names the kingdom, the provinces are my reading.

ledger.note: 1388: Ramesuan recovers Ayutthaya and Lavo is fully incorporated. The page: Ramesuan 'recovered it from Thong Lan in 1388' and 'Lavo was not fully incorporated into Ayutthaya's political order until 1388'; Cliopatria's Lavo row runs to 1394 and the Lavo cells join Ayutthaya's shape in 1395.

region.text: the whole of Lavo, fully incorporated

ledger.note: 1388: Ramesuan, the Lopburi king, is back on the throne of Ayutthaya, after Borommarachathirat's line (1370) and Thong Lan.
1393: Ramesuan besieges Angkor again. 'In 1393, the Ayutthayan king Ramesuan besieged Angkor again, capturing it the next year.' Mirrors khmer-empire /ledger/33.

region.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

ledger.note: 1394: Angkor falls to Ayutthaya. The Khmer page gives no end to the Siamese hold ('Ramesuan's son ruled Kambuja for a short time before being assassinated', undated), so the span is closed as a contest, not an occupation. Mirrors khmer-empire /ledger/34.

region.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

ledger.note: 1408: the Suphannabhum line regains the throne under Intharacha ('the Suphannabhum line regains the throne under Intharacha').

1431: Siamese forces take Angkor and seat a puppet. The page quotes Briggs: 'Once-in 1430-31 -the Siamese captured Angkor and seated a Siamese puppet on the throne'; the Ayutthaya page has Angkor attacked 'in the 1430s' with 'a short-lived puppet ruler', and the Borommarachathirat II page gives 1431 in its lead and 1433 in the body (the pages disagree by two years), adding that Ayutthaya 'did not permanently occupy Angkor'. Khmer Empire page: Ponhea Yat 'abandoned Angkor as indefensible' in 1431.

region.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

ledger.note: 1432: the Cambodians recover their capital. Briggs, quoted on the page: 'But the Cambodians reconquered their capital the next year'. The Khmer Empire dossier ends in 1431 and post-angkor-cambodia begins in 1432 under Ponhea Yat, so the counterpart string is the state that held Angkor when the occupation began; the page gives no other end.

region.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

ledger.note: 1438: the tribute ends in annexation. 'It remained a tributary state of Ayutthaya until it was annexed by the kingdom in 1438 after the death of Borommapan.'

region.text: southern Lan Na and the northern cities: Phrae, Nan, Sawankhalok, Chaliang, Chiang Mai

ledger.note: 1451: Sawankhalok breaks away to Lan Na. 'In 1451, Sawankhalok broke away from Ayutthaya and joined Lan Na, and thus the conflict between the two kingdoms broke out anew.' Region narrowed from all of Sukhothai province to the two towns (a 35 km circle round Sawankhalok); Sawankhalok is not yet in the gazetteer.

ledger.note: 1453 (placeholder for 1452-1458): Sawankhalok rejoins Ayutthaya. The war page dates no return; its 1459 sentence says Lan Na captured Sawankhalok 'which had in the meantime rejoined Ayutthaya' and the Tilokaraj page gives no events for 1451-1459. Page silent on the year; 1453 is the year after Ayutthaya's counter-offensive of 1452 (Chiang Mai taken and left).

ledger.note: 1459: Lan Na captures Sawankhalok again. 'In 1459, Lan Na captured Sawankhalok, which had in the meantime rejoined Ayutthaya.' Narrowed as in 1451; Ayutthaya's return is the 1474 gain.

region.text: Sawankhalok and Si Satchanalai (Chaliang), 35 km round Sawankhalok

ledger.note: 1459: Cliopatria adds the far south (Songkhla, Satun, Pattani: 32 cells, 18 of them in Kedah's outline). The page dates no southern conquest; it has expeditions down the peninsula in the 1290s-1490s. Page silent on 1459. Borommatrailokkanat page (read 2026-10-19): silent on Songkhla, Pattani, Satun and Kedah and on any event of 1459; it has envoys to Malacca in 1455 and 'In 1468, Borommatrailokkanat adopted a mandala tributary system', Nakhon Si Thammarat among the first-rank cities.

region.text: the peninsula south of Nakhon Si Thammarat, as Cliopatria draws 1459

ledger.note: 1460: Ayutthaya reconquers Phrae. 'A year later, Ayutthaya reconquered Phrae Province while Lan Na was engaged in conflict with the Shan states' ('a year later' than the 1459 Sawankhalok sentence).

region.text: Phrae Province

ledger.note: 1463: Borommatrailokkanat makes Phitsanulok the principal capital (infobox: Phitsanulok 1463-c.1488; the Sukhothai page: 'In 1463 Borommatrailokkanat moved the royal residence to Song Khwae').
1474: the war ends in stalemate. 'In 1474, Ayutthaya attacked Chienjuen and killed the governor of the city'; Lan Na retook it, 'putting an end to the conflict'. The page describes no treaty.

region.text: southern Lan Na and the northern cities

ledger.note: 1474: Ayutthaya takes Sawankhalok back. Tilokaraj page: 'Lan Na called the town Chiang Chuen while it held it'; 'Ayutthaya took it back in 1474 and peace followed the next year' (the sentence says 'it', which the summary placed after the Sawankhalok passage); Borommatrailokkanat page: 'In 1474, Borommatrailokkanat finally expelled Lan Na out of Ayutthaya territories'. The war page says instead that 'Lan Na then retook the city' in 1474 and lan-na-kingdom records the same disagreement; Sawankhalok is Ayutthaya's again by 1563 (Bayinnaung page).

region.text: Sawankhalok and Si Satchanalai (Chaliang), 35 km round Sawankhalok

ledger.note: c. 1488: the court returns to Ayutthaya (infobox: Ayutthaya 1488-early 1680s, Phitsanulok principal capital until c.1488).

1512 (Cliopatria's year): the Patani region is a tributary of Ayutthaya, drawn as a tint, not direct land. Patani page: 'The region had been subject to Siamese control for some time' before 1563, and 'The Siamese Ayutthaya Kingdom also conquered the isthmus during the 14th century'; the page gives no 1512 event and no tribute for Patani before 1584. Cliopatria draws the 36 cells (Narathiwat, Yala, Pattani) as Ayutthaya's from 1512. Replaces the earlier direct-land gain.

region.text: the Patani region

ledger.note: 1563: the Northern Cities fall to Toungoo as tributaries. 'The Burmese first took Phitsanulok, Sawankhalok, Kamphaeng Phet, Sukhothai thus turning them into tributary states' (the war that erupted in 1563); the Bayinnaung page has Kamphaeng Phet taken on 4 December 1563.

region.text: the Northern Cities of Sukhothai: Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Phichai, Sawankhalok, Kamphaeng Phet, Phichit and Phra Bang (the page's 1584 list), read as these provinces

ledger.note: 1563: Patani breaks with Ayutthaya. 'The sultan of Patani Mudhaffar Shah attacked Ayutthaya in 1563' (he died in 1564 on the way home). The page does not say tribute stopped; the end of the vassal span is my reading, and it explains why the Patani cells leave the outline (Cliopatria's Patani row begins in 1572). The next acknowledgement is 1584.

region.text: the Patani region

ledger.note: 1564: Ayutthaya surrenders to Bayinnaung and its western strip (Tenasserim, the Mon uplands) passes to Toungoo. 'The invaders finally captured the Portuguese ships and batteries on 7 February 1564'; 'The Siamese king surrendered on 18 February 1564'; infobox 'Suzerain of Siam: 18 February 1564'. The page gives the surrender, not the cession; the western strip is Cliopatria's 36 cells.

region.text: the western strip of Ayutthaya's 1563 outline: Tenasserim, Kayin and Mon uplands

ledger.note: 1568: Ayutthaya revolts and attacks Phitsanulok. 'The war began in 1568 when Ayutthaya unsuccessfully attacked Phitsanulok, a Burmese vassal state.'

region.text: Phitsanulok and Ayutthaya

ledger.note: 1569: Ayutthaya falls again to Bayinnaung. 'The city fell on that very night on 2 August 1569' (the 1568-1569 page gives 2 August 1569 as the defeat and 7 August as the night the gates were opened); 'Ayutthaya became a Burmese vassal state, with Mahathammarachathirat appointed king', named king of Siam on 29 September 1569.

region.text: Phitsanulok and Ayutthaya

ledger.note: 1584: Raja Hijau of Patani acknowledges Siamese authority. 'Raja Hijau came to the throne in 1584 and acknowledged Siamese authority.' The Patani page calls Ayutthaya's arrangement vassal states that kept their own affairs.

region.text: Patani

ledger.note: May 1584: Naresuan proclaims Ayutthaya's independence and the Northern Cities return. The Ayutthaya page: 'May 1584: Naresuan proclaims independence'; the Sukhothai page, infobox 'Annexed to Ayutthaya: 1584', and after the Sittaung battle 'Naresuan forcibly relocated people from the northern cities'.

region.text: the Northern Cities of Sukhothai: Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Phichai, Sawankhalok, Kamphaeng Phet, Phichit and Phra Bang (the page's 1584 list), read as these provinces

ledger.note: 1591: Siam invades Cambodia. 'Pursat and Battambang soon fell into Thai hands' and the Longvek citadel was besieged for three months before the Thais retreated (the page: infobox 'Dates: 1591 - 3 January 1594').

region.text: Pursat, Battambang and the Longvek citadel

ledger.note: 1593: Naresuan takes the Tenasserim coast. 'Tenasserim resisted the siege for 15 days while the siege of Tavoy lasted 20 days', both 'accepted Ayutthaya's overlordship'; Phraya Chakri then captured Mergui and the boats in its port.

region.text: the Tenasserim coast: Tavoy, Tenasserim and Mergui

ledger.note: 1594: the Mon provinces become Siamese. Phraya Si Salai with 3,000 men: 'the small Burmese garrison at Martaban abandoned the town'; 'The Mon provinces then became subject to Siam'.

region.text: Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces

ledger.note: 3 January 1594: Naresuan storms Longvek. 'On 3 January 1594, following an hour long artillery preparation, Naresuan's army stormed the city'; King Satha escaped into Laos.

region.text: Pursat, Battambang and the Longvek citadel

ledger.note: 1594: Cambodia passes under Ayutthaya's suzerainty. 'In 1594, Longvek was successfully captured and sacked by Siamese forces' and 'Cambodian royals were taken hostage and relocated to the court of Ayutthaya'; the war page says the royals were 'kept under permanent Siamese influence' and does not use the word vassal. The vassalage is my reading of the tribute that the page says Chey Chettha II stopped in 1618 and of the Ayutthaya page's 'lost suzerainty over ... Cambodia' under Songtham.

region.text: Cambodia under Siamese suzerainty after the fall of Longvek

ledger.note: January 1595: Naresuan marches on Pegu with 120,000 men. 'In January 1595, Naresuan led an army of 120,000 men from the Siamese capital', besieged Pegu about three months and withdrew; in 1597-1600 Pegu was abandoned and burned and he gave up at Toungoo.

region.text: Pegu and Toungoo

ledger.note: 1600: Lan Na comes into Siam's orbit. The war page has Naresuan seeking to 'regain some territories including Lan Na and Tanintharyi region' (the Ayutthaya page: in 1614 Burma 'invaded Lan Na, then a vassal of Ayutthaya'), and at Toungoo he was 'joined by his allies including the Viceroy of Chiang Mai'. The page gives no 1600-1602 date for Lan Na (the year is the war's end).

region.text: Lan Na

ledger.note: May 1600: Naresuan gives up the campaign. 'in May 1600, he gave up the fight' at Toungoo; the Toungoo empire ended in December 1600 when Natshinnaung killed Nanda Bayin.

region.text: Pegu and Toungoo

ledger.note: 1613: Burma takes Tavoy ('1613 Burma takes Tavoy'). The Anaukpetlun page (read 2026-10-19) says instead: 'In 1613-1614, Anaukpetlun attacked Dawei, Tenasserim and Chiang Mai but was repelled' (and, undated, that he reconquered 'the Upper Tenasserim'); the pages disagree and the Ayutthaya page's 1613 is kept.

region.text: Tavoy

ledger.note: 1618: the treaty gives Lan Na to Burma. '1614 Burma invades Lan Na'; '1618: treaty. Burma gains Lan Na; Ayutthaya keeps southern Tanintharyi'.

region.text: Lan Na

ledger.note: 1618: the Mon provinces are back under Burma by the Cliopatria shape of 1619 (222 cells). The page says only that the 1618 treaty leaves Ayutthaya 'southern Tanintharyi'; page silent on when the Mon provinces were lost. Anaukpetlun page (read 2026-10-19): silent on the Mon provinces; its 1618 line ('Burma would control Mottama and Thailand would control Chiang Mai') differs from the Ayutthaya page's treaty (Burma gains Lan Na); date stays a bridge.

region.text: Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces, taken in 1594 (Pegu and its delta were besieged but never held, so they are not part of this loss)

ledger.note: 1618: Cambodia stops paying tribute. 'In 1618, King Chey Chettha II stopped sending tribute to Ayutthaya and reasserted Cambodian independence'; the page adds that a Siamese expedition of 1621-22 'to reconquer Cambodia failed in dramatic fashion'.

region.text: Cambodia under Siamese suzerainty after the fall of Longvek

ledger.note: 1633: Ayutthaya attacks Patani and fails. The Patani page: 'prompted the Siamese to attack Patani in 1633-1634'; Siam failed to take it.

region.text: Patani

ledger.note: 1634: the attack on Patani ends without gain ('Siam failed to take Patani').

region.text: Patani

ledger.note: February 1663: Narai takes Chiang Mai. Narai's forces 'captured Chiang Mai in February 1663 before support from the Toungoo Empire was able to arrive' (the page gives February; the month is left out of the field because the end of the occupation has none).

region.text: Chiang Mai

ledger.note: 1663: the Siamese leave Lan Na 'later that year' because of a rebellious populace (no month on the page).

region.text: Chiang Mai

ledger.note: November 1663: Narai invades Burma in three columns. He 'launched a three-pronged invasion of Burma' with Tavoy, then Martaban and Moulmein as objectives; the page does not confirm Tavoy was taken.

union.text: the Tenasserim coast: Tavoy, Tenasserim and Mergui
Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces

region.text: the Tenasserim coast and the Mon provinces

ledger.note: 1664: the Siamese retreat. Rajanubhab's account has them withdraw 'until May 1664 when provisions became scarce'; the Tenasserim cities 'fell back almost immediately under Burmese rule'; Burma and Siam then had peace for 95 years.

union.text: the Tenasserim coast: Tavoy, Tenasserim and Mergui
Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces

region.text: the Tenasserim coast and the Mon provinces

ledger.note: c. 1680: the court moves to Lopburi. The infobox: Lopburi 'early 1680s-1688'; the year is a placeholder for 'early 1680s'. Narai page (read 2026-10-19): no year for the move ('arguably prompted by the Dutch naval blockade of Ayutthaya in 1664'); Narai is at his Lopburi palaces in 1685 and in March 1688.
1688: Patani refuses Phetracha. 'When Phetracha took control of Ayutthaya in 1688, Patani refused to acknowledge his authority and rebelled.'

region.text: Patani

ledger.note: 1688: the capital returns to Ayutthaya (infobox: Ayutthaya 1688-1767); Phetracha took the throne and was crowned on 1 August 1688.

1715: Ayutthaya invades Cambodia against Vietnamese backing. Ang Em page: 'in 1715, the Siamese king sent 100,500 (over 100,000) troops to invade Cambodia' while 'Annam sent 25,000 troops'; the Ayutthaya page: 'Ayutthaya fought the Nguyen Lords of southern Vietnam for control of Cambodia from around 1715'. The Ang Em page is internally inconsistent (troop and casualty figures) and the Post-Angkor page has nothing on 1715.

region.text: Cambodia

ledger.note: 1717 (end not dated by any page): the second Siamese invasion of 1717 ends and the Siamese withdraw. Ang Em page: 'The Siamese stopped the war and negotiated'; 'the remaining Siamese troops were withdrawn back to Ayutthaya'. The Siamese-Vietnamese wars table instead calls 1717 a Siamese victory ('Vietnam loses sovereignty over Cambodia but annexes several border provinces'); the pages disagree and no border change is recorded here.

region.text: Cambodia

ledger.note: December 1759: Alaungpaya invades. 'The Burmese vanguard conquered Tavoy in December', 'After taking the whole Tenasserim Coast' he crossed the hills in March 1760 and reached the outskirts of Ayutthaya in late March.

union.text: the Tenasserim coast: Tavoy, Tenasserim and Mergui

region.text: the Tenasserim coast and the hills to Ayutthaya

ledger.note: 1760: Burma keeps Dawei and upper Tenasserim. Infobox result: 'Inconclusive. Burmese gained Dawei and upper Tenasserim but failed to capture Ayutthaya'; Alaungpaya retreated in April and died in May 1760.

region.text: Dawei and upper Tenasserim

ledger.note: May 1760: the war ends with Alaungpaya's death near Martaban; Ayutthaya 'was thus saved from Burmese conquest' for seven years.

union.text: the Tenasserim coast: Tavoy, Tenasserim and Mergui

region.text: the Tenasserim coast and the hills to Ayutthaya

ledger.note: 1765: the rest of Tenasserim goes to Burma. 'Siam lost Tenaserim to Burma for perpetuity in 1765.'

region.text: the Tenasserim coast: Tavoy, Tenasserim and Mergui

ledger.note: 23 August 1765: the last Burmese invasion begins. Nemyo Thihapate 'descended onto Northern Siam in August 1765'; the southern army came by the Myitta Pass to Kanchanaburi; Lanna fell in August 1763 and Luang Prabang and Vientiane in March 1765.

region.text: northern and western Siam to the capital

ledger.note: 7 April 1767: the war ends with the fall of Ayutthaya (the war page runs 23 August 1765 - 7 April 1767).

region.text: northern and western Siam to the capital

ledger.note: 7 April 1767: Ayutthaya falls. 'For fourteen months, from February 1766 to April 1767, Ayutthaya endured the Burmese siege'; 'Ayutthaya, Siamese royal capital for four centuries, fell to the Burmese on 7 April 1767.' The Burmese occupied the ruins two months to June 1767; Phraya Tak 'reconquered Ayutthaya-Thonburi area in November 1767' and was enthroned in December 1767 at Thonburi.

region.text: what was left of the kingdom in 1766

wars.name: Ayutthaya-Angkor war (1352-1357)

zones.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

wars.outcome: Angkor was besieged in 1352 and captured the next year; Siamese princes were set on the Khmer throne until Suryavamsa Rajadhiraja retook it in 1357.
wars.note: Khmer Empire page: chronology table '1352-1357: Siamese Ayutthaya invasion led by Uthong'. The Ayutthaya page says only 'within a few years' of the founding and that the army took 'captives and goods rather than annexing the city'; the Ramathibodi I page has 'In 1352 he laid siege to Yasodharapura (Angkor)' and the throne kept 'until 1357'. Replaces the earlier bracket 1351-1355.

wars.name: Siamese capture of Angkor (1393-1394)

zones.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

wars.outcome: Ramesuan besieged Angkor in 1393 and captured it in 1394; the page does not say how long it was held.
wars.note: Khmer Empire page: 'In 1393, the Ayutthayan king Ramesuan besieged Angkor again, capturing it the next year'; chronology table '1393: Siamese Ayutthaya invasion led by Ramesuan'.

wars.name: Siamese attacks on Angkor (1431-1433)

zones.text: Angkor Thom (Nakhon Thom, Yasodharapura) and the Angkor heartland

wars.outcome: Ayutthaya attacked Angkor, did not sack it on the Ayutthaya page and installed a short-lived puppet ruler; the Khmer court left Angkor for Phnom Penh.
wars.note: The Ayutthaya page says only 'In the 1430s'. Post-Angkor page (Briggs): captured 1430-31, Cambodians 'reconquered their capital the next year'; Khmer Empire page: Ponhea Yat abandoned Angkor in 1431; Borommarachathirat II page: 1431 in the lead, 1433 for Sam Phraya's campaign in the body, a puppet (the Prince of Phrak) later assassinated by Ponhea Yat, undated. Years 1431-1433 span the pages; the ledger carries the occupation 1431-1432.

wars.name: Ayutthaya-Lan Na War

zones.text: southern Lan Na and the northern cities

wars.outcome: Stalemate; Lan Na 'achieved limited territorial gains' and ended the war by retaking Chienjuen in 1474.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1547-1549)
wars.outcome: The Burmese siege of Ayutthaya failed.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1563-1564)

zones.text: the Northern Cities of Sukhothai: Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Phichai, Sawankhalok, Kamphaeng Phet, Phichit and Phra Bang (the page's 1584 list), read as these provinces

wars.outcome: Bayinnaung took the Northern Cities (Kamphaeng Phet on 4 December 1563), captured the Portuguese ships and batteries on 7 February 1564 and received the Siamese king's surrender on 18 February 1564; Ayutthaya became his vassal.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1568-1569)
wars.outcome: Burmese victory: the city fell on 2 August 1569 and Mahathammarachathirat was made vassal king.
wars.note: Lan Xang is on Ayutthaya's side in the page's infobox; Burma occupied Lan Xang briefly until 1570.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1584-1593)
wars.outcome: Naresuan proclaimed independence in May 1584 and in 1593 killed Mingyi Swa in the elephant duel; Siam invaded Burma.
wars.note: Only the Ayutthaya page was read for this war; its own page was not opened (page budget).

wars.name: Siamese-Cambodian War (1591-1594)

zones.text: Pursat, Battambang and the Longvek citadel

wars.outcome: Siamese victory: Pursat and Battambang fell in 1591, Longvek was stormed on 3 January 1594 and Cambodian royals were taken to Ayutthaya.
wars.note: The page says the first column aimed at Siem Reap and Kampong Svay in 1593 but does not confirm their capture; Cliopatria's Ayutthaya shape of 1595 shows no Cambodian ground. The page gives conflicting Siamese casualty figures. Cambodia's later status is the vassal span 1594-1618 in the ledger.

Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces

wars.outcome: Inconclusive: Siam took the Tenasserim coast (1593) and the Mon provinces (1594), besieged Pegu in 1595 and gave up at Toungoo in May 1600.

wars.outcome: 'A Siamese expedition in 1621-22 to reconquer Cambodia failed in dramatic fashion'; no border moved.

wars.name: Siamese attack on Patani (1633-1634)
wars.outcome: The Siamese failed to take Patani.

Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces

zones.text: the Tenasserim coast, the Mon provinces and Chiang Mai

wars.outcome: Burmese defensive victory: Narai held Chiang Mai from February 1663 to later that year and withdrew from Burma by May 1664; the Tenasserim cities fell back under Burmese rule almost at once.

wars.name: Siamese-Nguyen struggle for Cambodia (1715-1717)
wars.outcome: Disputed: the Ang Em page has the Siamese invasions of 1715 and 1717 fail and withdraw; the Siamese-Vietnamese wars table calls 1717 a Siamese victory. No border change is recorded.
wars.note: Ayutthaya page: 'Ayutthaya fought the Nguyen Lords of southern Vietnam for control of Cambodia from around 1715', no end date. The Ang Em page's figures are internally inconsistent; treat the years, not the numbers, as the page's.

wars.outcome: Inconclusive: Burma gained Dawei and upper Tenasserim but failed to take Ayutthaya; Alaungpaya died in May 1760.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1765-1767)
wars.outcome: Burmese victory: Ayutthaya fell on 7 April 1767 after a fourteen-month siege; Siam lost Tenasserim; Taksin reconquered the Ayutthaya-Thonburi area in November 1767.

certainty.note: A mandala of tributary cities with no treaty lines: the page's frontiers are cities and expeditions. The nearest to a settlement is the 1618 treaty (Lan Na to Burma, southern Tanintharyi kept), which names no boundary.

notes:
Cliopatria's single Ayutthaya row 1352-1768 is one state; its final shapes run a year past the fall (7 April 1767) and the Thonburi row starts in 1769.

Findings against Cliopatria: (1) 1352-1374 is a 7,488 km2 core, and the 1375 shape jumps to 288,685 km2 with no event on any page opened; the jump takes 680 cells from Cliopatria's Sukhothai outline of 1374, 212 from the Khmer Empire and 13 from Lavo, so it is a tributary sphere, flagged confidence 1. (2) Cliopatria draws the Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Kamphaeng Phet, ...) as Ayutthaya's from 1375, although the Sukhothai page has Sukhothai a tributary 1378-1438 and its capital at Song Khwae (Phitsanulok) to 1438: corrected to a vassal tint until 1438. The Sukhothai dossier (another group) draws Sukhothai's core as Tak, Nan, Lampang, Phrae, Uttaradit, which does not include Phitsanulok: the two dossiers should be reconciled. (3) Bago and Yangon cells in the 1595 and 1600 shapes are not supported (Pegu was besieged and abandoned, never held). (4) The 1662-1669 Mon strip and the 1752-1761 Kayin/Mon strip are not supported by the war pages. (5) The 1691 shape hands the Patani region back to Ayutthaya because Cliopatria's Patani row ends in 1690; the Patani page has the sultanate rebel in 1688 and last to 1786. (6) No shape for 1572-1587 (Toungoo vassalage and independence): new keyframes.

Pages: nine pages for Ayutthaya (Ayutthaya Kingdom, Sukhothai Kingdom, Ayutthaya-Lan Na War, five Burmese-Siamese war pages, Patani Kingdom) plus Bayinnaung, opened for the Shan States and used here for the 1564 and 1569 dates. Events and wars not tied to a page of their own: the Angkor wars (Ayutthaya page only, undated), the 1584-1593 war (Ayutthaya page only). The Ayutthaya-Lan Na War URL with an en dash returned 404; the hyphen form loaded.
